solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

blocks.note: odd or weird, the everyday sense
belonging to one person alone, as in a habit special to someone

explanation.walkthrough: Two words, two senses: the odd one, and the older sense of 'belonging only to', as in 'a custom peculiar to Cornwall'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both odd and particular to one person, so each clue word is a synonym for one sense.

clue.text: Suspect crept in on US university

indicators.note: as an adjective, suspect means dodgy or not to be trusted, so the letters are not in their proper order

blocks.note: nine letters of fodder, all three words

explanation.surface: A suspect has sneaked onto an American campus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suspect' reads as a noun, the intruder, but it is an adjective telling you to rearrange CREPT IN ON.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the Ivy League institution in New Jersey, an example of an American seat of learning.

blocks.note: to con someone is to cheat them
British slang: someone with form has a criminal record

explanation.surface: A police warning to keep an eye on a swindler with a criminal record.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Follow' looks like tailing a suspect, but it means going along with rules. In British usage 'form' is a criminal record.
explanation.definitionFit: To follow rules or custom is to comply with them, a close synonym in the sense of obeying.

clue.text: A posh girl lying about extremely costly gift

indicators.note: lying down and turned about suggests something laid flat and facing the other way
the extremes of a word are its two ends, so keep just the outside letters

blocks.note: A plus GEL, the plummy upper-class pronunciation of girl
first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: A well-bred young woman fibbing about how much an expensive present cost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lying' tempts you to think of fibbing, but together with 'about' it turns A GEL round to LEGA. 'Gel' is how a posh English speaker says girl.
explanation.definitionFit: A bequest left in a will is money or property handed on freely, a kind of present.

clue.text: Bruised old pal’s ego? I express regret

indicators.note: something bruised has been knocked about and damaged, so its letters are battered out of shape

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
keep the S of the possessive
used as it stands
used as it stands

explanation.surface: Someone who has hurt an old friend's pride saying sorry.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'I' does double work in the surface, as the speaker, but it is anagram fodder with O, PALS and EGO.
explanation.definitionFit: To say sorry for a wrong is to voice remorse, a straight synonym for the verb phrase.

blocks.note: standard abbreviation, as in genealogies
rings as circular bands

explanation.surface: Someone weeps every time their wife phones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rings' reads as telephoning, but it is a noun: circles, i.e. hoops.
explanation.definitionFit: Loud shouts of excitement or delight are plural nouns for shrieks, matching the plural noun.

blocks.note: surface reading: a man grumbling that his wife is behind schedule again
setter's reading: late as in deceased, so this man has lost his spouse

explanation.surface: A husband irritated that his wife is running late.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition. 'Late' means dead, as in 'the late Queen', and 'unfortunately' becomes sympathy rather than irritation.
explanation.definitionFit: A man whose spouse has died is exactly what this noun names, so the sentence describes him.

clue.text: Errant peer loves to stay in bed too long

indicators.note: errant means straying from the proper course, so the letters wander out of place

blocks.note: nine letters of fodder, both words

explanation.surface: A wayward lord who likes a long lie-in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peer' looks like a person, a member of the House of Lords, but it is only letters to rearrange with LOVES.
explanation.definitionFit: Failing to wake at the intended time means lying beyond when you meant to rise, a plain paraphrase.

blocks.note: to go by something is to go past it
the Ure is a river in North Yorkshire, a crossword favourite

explanation.surface: A field for cattle next to a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By' reads as 'beside', but here it means 'past'. The Ure is a river in North Yorkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: Fields where livestock feed on growing grass are what the noun names, a direct synonym.

blocks.note: fashionable, up to date, as in 'the in thing'
read as new's, i.e. new is: N is the standard abbreviation for new, and the 's is dropped

explanation.surface: The neighbourhood pub is where you hear the latest gossip.
explanation.walkthrough: A local is British slang for your regular neighbourhood pub. 'Current' suggests electricity (I), but here it means fashionable.
explanation.definitionFit: The British call their nearest regular pub their local, and a pub or tavern is this kind of establishment.

indicators.note: criminal means lawless and wrong, so the letters break the rules of their order

blocks.note: ten letters of fodder, both words

explanation.surface: A lawyer doubts the charge that someone resold firearms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Criminal' looks like a noun, the gun dealer, but it is an adjective saying the letters of RESOLD GUNS go astray.
explanation.definitionFit: An accusation without any basis in evidence has not been established, so both mean lacking support.

clue.text: Express perhaps in language of the young?

definitions.text: Express perhaps in language of the young?

blocks.clueFragment: Express perhaps in language of the young
blocks.note: surface reading: how teenagers might phrase something, their slang
setter's reading: an express is a fast train, and small children have their own nursery word for a train

explanation.surface: A question about how young people put things into words.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Express' looks like a verb, to put into words, but it is a noun: an express train, named in baby talk.
explanation.definitionFit: Small children call a railway engine by this imitative nursery word, and an express is one kind of locomotive.

clue.text: Get to know Kiwi’s euphemisms to an extent

indicators.note: only partly, so you want a part of the words that follow rather than the whole

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: Learning to understand the polite phrases New Zealanders use.
explanation.walkthrough: The run starts inside KIWI'S and ends inside EUPHEMISMS; the apostrophe is ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: To become aware of the truth is to learn about it, an informal phrasal verb for finding out.

clue.text: Where you might end up, in doctor’s opinion

blocks.note: with 'opinion' after it, 'in the opinion of' can be put as 'to', as in 'it seems fine to me'
Bachelor of Medicine, a doctor's qualification
completes the phrase begun by 'in'; it adds no letters of its own

explanation.surface: A patient told by a doctor where they will finish up.
explanation.walkthrough: MB is Bachelor of Medicine, a doctor's qualification. 'To' carries the sense of 'in the view of', as in 'it seems fine to me'.
explanation.definitionFit: A burial vault is where a body finally rests, so it is where everyone eventually finishes.

blocks.note: to stop something is to block it
the head of an organisation is its boss

explanation.surface: Preventing the manager from getting hold of drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dope' reads as drugs, but it is a person: a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal insults for a stupid person, making them synonyms for someone slow-witted.

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
used as it stands
to charge someone to do something is to order it

explanation.surface: A disturbed young woman is formally accused of a crime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charged' suggests an arrest, but it means 'commanded', as in 'charged with a duty'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both describe a mind thrown into confusion or disturbance, a synonym for being mentally unbalanced.

blocks.note: old boy, a former pupil of a school
a retainer is a long-serving household servant

explanation.surface: A loyal old boy has been given a butler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retainer' could be a fee or a dental brace; here it is the old word for a domestic servant.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who keeps religious rules or customs carefully is conscientious in following them, the sense shared here.

blocks.note: a dam is an animal's mother
a direct synonym

explanation.surface: Someone swears at their motherland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Curses' looks like a verb, but it is the exclamation 'Curses!', which the answer can also be.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are old-fashioned exclamations of annoyance, interchangeable oaths uttered when something goes wrong.

definitions.note: a phrase, an imperative the writer disregarded

blocks.note: plain, businesslike, without frills
Edward Lear popularised the limerick and is famous for his nonsense verse, so he never obeyed a ban on it

explanation.surface: A plain-speaking rule that a comic poet chose to disregard.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as two words, an order banning silliness; Edward Lear, the great limerick writer, published 'A Book of Nonsense'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone direct and practical, without fuss or frivolity, is described by this compound adjective.

clue.text: Look after Ohio cleric going around diocese

indicators.note: to go around is to turn back on yourself, so the word faces the other way

blocks.note: the postal abbreviation for Ohio is OH; the first letter serves here as a standard short form
short for Reverend, a clergyman's title
a bishop's see is his diocese

explanation.surface: A priest in Ohio tours his diocese to look after it.
explanation.walkthrough: A see is the area a bishop governs; the Holy See is the Pope's.
explanation.definitionFit: To supervise work is to take charge of it and watch over it, a synonym for managing.

clue.text: Nurse American politician briefly, one in upper house

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, so the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: State Enrolled Nurse, a former British nursing grade
standard abbreviation
Tory, a British Conservative, cut to three letters

explanation.surface: A nurse and an American politician, one of whom sits in a senate.
explanation.walkthrough: SEN is the old British grade State Enrolled Nurse; a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of a senate sits in the upper chamber of a legislature, such as the US Congress.

blocks.note: surface reading: a compact people carrier, the British name for a minivan
setter's reading: small people are babies, and this carries them about

explanation.surface: A compact family car.
explanation.walkthrough: A people carrier is British for a minivan. Regroup as 'small-people carrier' and it is a baby's pushchair.
explanation.definitionFit: A British baby carriage is pushed along carrying infants, who are literally small people.

clue.text: Desert people’s daily struggle to survive

blocks.note: to rat on someone is to desert or betray them
a race is a people, and the ’s stands for 'is', joining to the definition

explanation.surface: Nomads of the desert struggle each day just to stay alive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Desert' reads as sand dunes, but it is a verb: to abandon, which is to rat.
explanation.definitionFit: The exhausting competitive grind of modern working life is an idiom for relentless, pointless striving.

blocks.note: the person who wrote this crossword, speaking of themself
a breed of gun dog, such as the Irish or English one

explanation.walkthrough: Crossword compilers often refer to themselves in clues as 'me' or 'this setter'; the question mark flags the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: A crossword compiler and a breed of gun dog share one name, so each half points there.

clue.text: Judge embarrassed for the most part, no barrister returning

indicators.note: most but not all of a word is kept, so the final letter drops off
coming back the way it went, so the letters run from the other end

blocks.note: RED, as a blushing face, minus its last letter
NO plus KC, King's Counsel, a senior barrister

explanation.surface: A judge is red-faced that no barrister has come back to court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Judge' looks like the person on the bench, but it is a verb: to estimate. KC is King's Counsel, a senior British barrister.
explanation.definitionFit: To estimate or form an opinion is to consider or calculate, a synonym for the verb.

indicators.note: something surprising comes out in an unexpected way, so the letters are unpredictably arranged

blocks.note: eight letters of fodder

explanation.surface: A teenager unexpectedly whips up a wholesome beverage.
explanation.walkthrough: One word gives all eight letters, which is easy to miss when it looks like the subject of the sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: Unfermented Chinese brew is widely promoted for antioxidants and wellness benefits, an example of a nourishing beverage.

definitions.note: a phrase describing what the answer does

blocks.note: a beloved partner
read as two words: the heart, or middle letter, of the five-letter word SWEET

explanation.walkthrough: An E could be ecstasy, the drug, which a girlfriend might slip you; really it is the central letter of 'sweet', its heart.
explanation.definitionFit: A term of affection for a romantic partner, used for the woman someone is courting.

indicators.note: to shift is to move to a new place, so one letter changes position in the word

blocks.note: to ail is to trouble, as in 'what ails you'
L, from Latin libra, is the pound; it names the letter that moves, adding nothing new

explanation.surface: A fighter struggling to lose weight before the weigh-in.
explanation.walkthrough: Muhammad Ali was the heavyweight champion. Move the L (pounds) in AIL one place along.
explanation.definitionFit: Muhammad Ali, the famous American heavyweight champion, is an example of a prizefighter.

definitions.note: a phrase for the person doing the seducing

blocks.note: a bedmaker, who cleans students' rooms at Cambridge colleges
whimsically, one who beds someone

explanation.surface: A college cleaner caught up in a seduction scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: At Cambridge a bedder is the cleaner who tidies students' rooms; the question mark flags the invented second sense of someone who takes people to bed.
explanation.definitionFit: The university's domestic staff who make beds are called by this name; to bed someone is to seduce them.

clue.text: Medic eating bit of trout and other fish

indicators.note: whatever eats something takes it inside, so one piece swallows another
just a small bit is kept, the opening letter

blocks.note: a doctor who operates
the first letter only

explanation.surface: A doctor dining on some trout and another fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Other fish' is the definition: trout is one fish, the answer another. The surface makes 'fish' sound like part of the meal.
explanation.definitionFit: A large bony fish prized as the source of caviar is a different species from trout.
